Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-29
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 56 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Wu (Redwood SE), Caleb Morris (Product), Tom Keller (Luminary CTO), Mira Chen (Lead ML Eng), Jose Alvarez (SRE), Priya Nair (Data Platform)

Auto-generated summary:
- Technical deep dive on tenant prefetch heuristics, cache key strategy, collision/eviction safety, and graceful degradation for multi-tenant KV/prefix cache.
- Agreed next steps: run hit-rate sims, share benchmark spreadsheet, provision VPC pilot, and align on SLOs for pilot.

Topics:
- Workload characterization and hotset identification
- Prefix/key synthesis and entropy controls
- Prefetch heuristics and TTL strategies
- Eviction policies and tenant isolation (soft vs hard siloing)
- Graceful degradation: model fallback, batching throttles, and cached partial responses
- VPC/on-prem considerations and encryption/KMS implications

Action items (auto): see metadata action_items field

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we wanted to run through the prefetch heuristics and how we think about graceful degradation when cache hit-rates drop. Tom, Mira, Jose—thanks for making the time.
[00:12] Tom Keller: Yeah thanks Ava, excited to dig in. We have a pretty bursty traffic pattern, smallish prompts but lots of short sessions - chat style. Our current infra is k8s on AWS, everything behind our VPC.
[00:22] Mira Chen: To add, our golden paths are about 70% repeated prefixes from support dialogs and internal docs, but the long tail is huge. We want to prioritize the hotset without leaking cross-tenant context.
[00:36] Ravi Patel: Got it. Quick framing: Redwood's runtime supports prefix KV caching + prefetch. The key decisions are how you synthesize the cache key (prompt signature, normalized tokens, tenant salt), the TTL and prefetch window, and whether you allow shared hotset vs per-tenant silo.
[00:50] Jose Alvarez: Two immediate asks: 1) we need strong tenant isolation for PII flows, and 2) we can't have cache keys that accidentally re-identify or leak. So hashing and encryption are non-negotiable.
[01:05] Lena Wu: Totally—our approach is to salt keys with tenant ID and then run a keyed HMAC prior to hashing. That gives per-tenant namespace without storing tenant in plain text on the cache nodes. We also apply collision-resistant hash (we typically use xxhash64 with a prefix) but note xxhash is not crypto grade so we use an HMAC wrapper.
[01:22] Tom Keller: Quick Q: does that prevent shared hotset? We hoped to save cost by sharing top prompts across tenants for similar domains.
[01:30] Ravi Patel: Short answer: you can do a hybrid. Shared hotset gives better unit cost but increases risk of information leakage unless you canonicalize prompts at higher-level and strip tenant-specific tokens. A hybrid we often propose is a two-tier cache: a tenant-prefixed cache plus a shared anonymized hotset where keys are from normalized, de-identified prompt fingerprints.
[01:53] Priya Nair: How do you normalize without changing semantics? Our prompts include product names and customer ids.
[02:00] Lena Wu: We have a small normalization pipeline: replace high-entropy tokens with placeholders (e.g., <PRODUCT>, <ACCOUNT>), then hash the normalized token sequence. That pipeline runs in a lightweight preprocessor, can be on the edge or as a pre-request lambda. There will be some lossiness but we tune it to keep semantics for intent matching.
[02:19] Mira Chen: That sounds useful. What about hit-rate expectations? Luminary's analyst said 70% repeated prefixes but is that enough to justify prefetch complexity?
[02:27] Ravi Patel: We ran a sample on a customer with similar chat patterns—when hotset is 3-5% of unique prefixes but accounts for 50-60% of traffic, prefetch and KV caching reduced p99 latency by about 30% and token cost by 25% due to less repeated decoding. But results vary: important to simulate with your real prefix distribution.
[02:47] Tom Keller: Okay we'll share the sample distribution. Can you walk through eviction policies? If we get tenant storms, we don't want tenant A evicting B's hot keys.
[02:58] Ava Martinez: Two options: strict per-tenant shards (hard silo) or shared pool with weighted fairness. Hard siloing is simpler for compliance—each tenant's cache capacity is reserved; shared pool is more cost-efficient but requires eviction quotas and soft guarantees.
[03:15] Jose Alvarez: For us, compliance favors hard siloing for any workloads touching PII. Maybe for non-sensitive workloads we can opt into shared pooling.
[03:25] Caleb Morris: Another pattern is dynamic tenant throttling—if tenant A consumes more than their allocation, we degrade to model-bypass or reduce prefetch aggressiveness rather than let it evict others.
[03:38] Mira Chen: What graceful degradation strategies do you recommend? We worry about tail latency spikes during peak.
[03:44] Ravi Patel: Several levers: 1) model fallback—route to smaller / cheaper model when latency budget is tight; 2) partial response from cache—return a cached prefix and stream the rest; 3) per-request batching cap—limit batch size to keep p99 bounded; 4) preemptive cancellation of low-priority requests. We also use adaptive batching based on queue depth and SLOs.
[04:05] Tom Keller: Any real-world tradeoffs? For example, falling back to a smaller model—how much quality loss?
[04:12] Lena Wu: It depends. In our measurements, going from a 13B to a 6B recaster (not our official names) reduced latency by ~40% but has a measurable drop in factuality on multi-hop prompts. For short instruction-completion patterns it's often acceptable. So define success criteria per route.
[04:30] Priya Nair: Security: if we have a VPC/on-prem pilot, how are cache nodes provisioned? And how do we handle encryption at rest and in transit?
[04:38] Ravi Patel: For Private/VPC we run dedicated cache nodes inside your VPC; data at rest uses your KMS keys and disk encryption. In transit we use mTLS between runtime and cache. For Hosted shared infra we encrypt with provider-managed KMS but can bring-your-own-key for Dedicated/Private.
[04:55] Jose Alvarez: Audit logs? We need to trace cache operations for compliance.
[05:00] Ava Martinez: We capture cache ops in the Redwood Console—miss/hit logs, key namespaces (hashed), and request traces. We can increase retention for pilot accounts and integrate with your SIEM via syslog or S3 export.
[05:12] [05:12] Tom Keller: That helps. Next, prefetch heuristics—how do you decide which prefixes to prefetch and when?
[05:20] Ravi Patel: We use a score combining recent frequency, recency (LRU), and predicted next-token entropy. For chat scenarios we also prefer prefixes that frequently appear at start of session (session-entry hotset). Prefetch windows are adaptive: aggressive during steady-state, conservative under high pressure.
[05:38] Mira Chen: Predicted token entropy—how expensive is that to compute?
[05:42] Lena Wu: It's a lightweight estimator using a tiny n-gram model or a micro-ML model trained on your corpora. It runs in-line in the request path but is optimized to be low latency. We can also run it as an offline job and mark candidates for prefetch.
[05:56] Jose Alvarez: Can prefetch cause unnecessary cost? If we prefetch too much we pay for model forward passes.
[06:01] Ravi Patel: Yes, it's a tradeoff. Prefetch pays when hit-rate on prefetched items exceeds a threshold—our tooling computes ROI curves: e.g., if prefetch reduces downstream generation by X tokens per minute at Y cents per token, it's worth it. We'll share the ROI spreadsheet (action item).
[06:16] [06:16] Tom Keller: On KV key synthesis, are there common misconfigurations to watch for?
[06:20] Lena Wu: A few: including user-specific IDs in the clear, not normalizing whitespace/tokenization differences, and using short hash outputs that increase collision risk. Also mixing multiple normalization pipelines across services leads to cache fragmentation.
[06:34] Mira Chen: Collision risk—what happens on collision? Is there a safe fallback?
[06:38] Ravi Patel: If two different logical prompts map to same key, you get semantic leakage. We mitigate via: 1) using long hash outputs + HMAC; 2) key-versioning and checksum of payload; 3) storing small signature metadata with cached value so on read we validate the normalized fingerprint. If mismatch, treat as miss and optionally escalate to strict logging.
[06:57] Tom Keller: Nice. Regarding tenant storms, how do we detect and mitigate?
[07:03] Jose Alvarez: We already have rate alerts in our infra, but at cache layer we need per-tenant telemetry to trigger throttles.
[07:09] Ravi Patel: We emit per-tenant hit/miss and eviction metrics at fixed granularity. Mitigations: reduce prefetch window for offending tenant, limit background prefetch threads, or temporarily route heavy tenant to dedicated capacity.
[07:25] Priya Nair: How intrusive is moving a tenant to dedicated capacity? We worried about cutover complexity.
[07:30] Ava Martinez: The orchestration supports live migration: you provision dedicated pool, new requests are routed there, and a warmup prefetch is run to fill cache. There's some coordination but we aim for sub-hour cutovers for standard workloads.
[07:44] [07:44] Mira Chen: Can we simulate a tenant storm in your environment before pilot?
[07:48] Ravi Patel: Yes—we can run synthetic traffic replay into test clusters to validate eviction behavior and SLOs. Action item for us to run a runbook and share results.
[07:57] Tom Keller: On quantization and batching—do lower-precision models affect prefix cache behaviour?
[08:03] Lena Wu: Quantization affects decode determinism only slightly; cached outputs are model-agnostic if you store the raw logits or token sequences. But quantization might change top-k probabilities so for deterministic reuse you should cache the token prefix rather than logits. Also, some quantized paths are faster which reduces benefit of caching for short prompts.
[08:24] Jose Alvarez: For batching, we need to understand p99 behavior under our traffic. What's Redwood's approach?
[08:29] Ravi Patel: Continuous batching with latency-aware thresholds. We batch until a token-window or latency threshold is hit. For SLO-sensitive routes we cap batch size lower and increase instance count. We also support prioritized queues so interactive traffic bypasses large batch queues.
[08:44] Mira Chen: Is there tooling to tune batch size? We don't want to guess.
[08:47] Ava Martinez: Yes—Redwood Optimize will recommend batching profiles based on your traffic traces. We'll run its suggestion as part of the pilot.
[08:55] [08:55] Tom Keller: Security again: for on-prem cache nodes do you support HSM-backed keys?
[09:00] Ravi Patel: Yes—HSM/KMS integration is supported for Private deployments. Keys stay in your control.
[09:06] Priya Nair: Ok, let's talk about observability—what's visible in the Console and what we need to forward to our SIEM?
[09:13] Lena Wu: Console shows per-route token cost, p50/p95/p99 latencies, cache hit/miss rates, prefetch ROI, and eviction metrics. For your SIEM we can export detailed event logs including hashed key ids, tenant id (hashed), and decision traces.
[09:29] Jose Alvarez: Great. A small thing: please avoid logging prompt text in clear anywhere in exports.
[09:33] Ava Martinez: Absolutely—we never log raw prompts in audit exports; only hashed fingerprints and metadata unless you opt-in for debug with DPA.
[09:42] [09:42] Tom Keller: What's the recommended TTL strategy? Static vs adaptive TTL?
[09:46] Ravi Patel: Adaptive TTL usually wins. We compute TTL based on access frequency and recency; hot items have longer TTL, cold items shorter. Also use sliding TTL that refreshes on hits. For highly dynamic domains, short TTLs with aggressive prefetch is better.
[10:03] Mira Chen: How do you prevent cache amplification—if TTL refresh on hit keeps an item forever?
[10:08] Lena Wu: We bound sliding TTL with a max lifetime and track overall access rate. If an item is artificially refreshed by bots, we put a decay factor.
[10:17] Tom Keller: Any recommendations for storing per-prefix quality metrics (e.g., hallucination rate) and tying that into prefetch logic?
[10:23] Ravi Patel: We recommend a quality score pipeline: evaluate outputs against prompt testsets and record regression metrics per prefix. Prefetch candidates below a quality threshold are deprioritized. Redwood Optimize can automate this.
[10:38] [10:38] Priya Nair: About rollout: if we change normalization rules, we risk cache fragmentation. How do we handle migrations?
[10:44] Ava Martinez: Plan migrations with versioned keys. When rules change, increment key version so old entries expire, and run a backfill job to repopulate new keys for hotset. We also recommend A/B key-version rollout and monitor miss-rate spikes.
[11:00] Tom Keller: That makes sense. Can you show us a sample backfill/runbook?
[11:05] Ravi Patel: We'll attach a runbook and backfill script. Action item: share doc.
[11:09] [11:09] Discussion shifts to pilot logistics
[11:10] Ava Martinez: Proposed pilot scope: 2-week VPC pilot with 1 dedicated cache shard, prefetch enabled on two high-importance routes, and monitoring retention increased to 90 days.
[11:19] Tom Keller: Sounds fine. What's the expected cost ballpark?
[11:23] Caleb Morris: For a pilot at this scale expect a delta of about $X–Y/day; we'll share exact pricing in SOW. Pilot cost depends on instance types and prefetch workload.
[11:33] Mira Chen: Our main acceptance criteria: p99 latency <= 450ms for interactive routes, cache hit-rate >= 35% on targeted routes, no cross-tenant leakage, and runbook for tenant storm mitigation.
[11:45] Ava Martinez: We'll codify those as SLOs in the pilot doc.
[11:49] Jose Alvarez: Final question—do you have any known production incidents around prefix caching we should be aware of?
[11:55] Ravi Patel: A few learnings: 1) inconsistent normalization across microservices caused fragmentation; 2) very long TTLs without guardrails led to stale prefetched content after model updates; 3) insufficient per-tenant telemetry hid storms. All of these are solvable with the ops patterns we discussed.
[12:12] Tom Keller: That honesty is helpful. Ok next step—I'll share the anonymized prefix list and traffic samples by Tuesday.
[12:20] Ava Martinez: Great. We'll run the hit-rate sim and share the benchmark sheet, plus SOW/pricing. Any other questions?
[12:28] Priya Nair: One minor: can you include an example of the key hashing scheme in the runbook?
[12:32] Lena Wu: Yes we'll include pseudo-code and recommended libs.
[12:36] Caleb Morris: Also we'll include suggested monitor dashboards and alert thresholds.
[12:40] Tom Keller: Thanks all, appreciate the practicality here.
[12:44] Ava Martinez: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with artifacts and schedule the pilot kickoff.
[12:48] [12:48] Meeting end
